advances: Actual global counterexample to unconditional same-parity exclusion for faceted fibers, even with common oriented active caps. Its normalized depth is above the sharper $gamma_d/4$ target and the locked weak target.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
All inequalities defining $C$ are affine and the origin is interior. For $q=-1,0,1$, the complete integer rows have $p=-7,\dots,7$, $p=-4,\dots,4$ and $p=-1,0,1$ respectively, and their interval half-widths are $1,8/5,11/5$. These are all the sampled fibers and the total length is $15\cdot2+9\cdot16/5+3\cdot22/5=72$.

**Global upper bound.** The caps $H_\pm=\{\pm x+q\ge0\}$ each capture lengths $0,8/5,16/5$ per fiber in the three rows, so each has mass $24$. They cover the middle row. The two caps $\{\pm x-3(q+1)\ge0\}$ each capture half of every bottom fiber and exclude the other rows, so each has mass $15$. The two caps $\{\pm x+3(q-1)\ge0\}$ each capture half of every top fiber and exclude the other rows, so each has mass $33/5$. The exclusions use $11/5<3$. Together these six closed caps cover every point and give the global upper bound. In a product with $L$ they still cover and their masses multiply by $|L|$.

**All tilts at the outer mark.** For real $a,b,c$ let $F(a,b,c)$ be the mass in $C$ of the margin $x+a(p-1)+bq+c\ge0$. With $[v]_0^m=\max(0,\min(m,v))$, its exact expression is
$$
\begin{aligned}
F(a,b,c)&=\sum_{k=-8}^{6}[1+ak-b+c]_0^2
+\sum_{k=-5}^{3}[8/5+ak+c]_0^{16/5}\\
&\quad+\sum_{k=-2}^{0}[11/5+ak+b+c]_0^{22/5}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here $k=p-1$. For $a\ge0$, reflection $p\mapsto-p$ turns the margin with slope $-a$ into the margin with slope $a$ plus $2a$, so $F(-a,b,c)\ge F(a,b,c)$. Assume $a\ge0$.

Let $B_a$ be the distribution of $x+ak$ on the disjoint bottom intervals $k=-8,\dots,6$, $x\in[-1,1]$. Let $T_a$ be the distribution of $x+aj$ on the three intervals $j=0,1,2$, $x\in[-11/5,11/5]$. Each source has unit length density, and both distributions are atomless. Reflecting the top coordinate $x$ and writing $j=-k$ on that row shows that the two outer rows contribute $B_a([b-c,\infty))+66/5-T_a([b+c,\infty))$.

For all real $t$, $B_a([t,\infty))\ge T_a([t,\infty))-\Delta(a)$ where $\Delta(a)=3(6/5-4a)_+$. To see this, send the target intervals into the bottom intervals by the following piecewise translations. Each row gives the target label, its source range, the receiving label, and the shift of $x$.

| $j$ | Source range | $k$ | Shift |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $[-11/5,-1/5]$ | $0$ | $6/5$ |
| $0$ | $[-1/5,1/5]$ | $1$ | $1/5$ |
| $1$ | $[-11/5,-6/5]$ | $1$ | $6/5$ |
| $1$ | $[-6/5,-3/5]$ | $1$ | $8/5$ |
| $1$ | $[-3/5,1/5]$ | $2$ | $4/5$ |
| $2$ | $[-11/5,-1]$ | $2$ | $6/5$ |
| $2$ | $[-1,1/5]$ | $3$ | $4/5$ |
| $0,1,2$ | $[1/5,11/5]$ | $j+4$ | $-6/5$ |

The ranges partition the three targets up to endpoints. The images in $k=0$ fill $[-1,1]$, in $k=1$ give $[0,2/5],[-1,0],[2/5,1]$, in $k=2$ give $[1/5,1],[-1,1/5]$, and in $k=3$ give $[-1/5,1]$. Each of $k=4,5,6$ receives $[-1,1]$. All pieces are disjoint up to endpoints within each receiving interval. The first seven rows have nonnegative shift and $k\ge j$, so they do not lose any points in the tail. Each of the three pieces in the last row has projected displacement $4a-6/5$. Its possible loss at any one threshold is at most $(6/5-4a)_+$ because it has unit length density. This proves the tail estimate.

**Paired threshold bound.** Adding the two outer-row masses at $c$ and $-c$ and applying the tail estimate at $b-c$ and $b+c$ gives at least $132/5-2\Delta(a)$. Write $h_0=8/5$ and $\phi(v)=[h_0+v]_0^{2h_0}$. The paired middle-row terms with $-3\le k\le3$ total $112/5$ since $\phi(v)+\phi(-v)=2h_0$. For each remaining $k=-K$, with $K=4,5$, the two terms total at least $2(h_0-Ka)_+$. Indeed, set $v=h_0-Ka$. If $v\le0$ the lower bound is zero. If $0<v\le h_0$ and $|c|\le v$, neither value $v\pm c$ exceeds $2h_0$, and their sum is $2v$. If $|c|>v$ the larger clipped value alone is at least $2v$. Therefore
$$
\tfrac12\bigl[F(a,b,c)+F(a,b,-c)\bigr]
\ge56/5+(8/5-4a)_++(8/5-5a)_++66/5-\Delta(a).
$$
For $0\le a\le3/10$ the right side is $24+3a$, and for $a\ge3/10$ it is at least $122/5$. Reflection extends the bound $24$ to every real $a$.

**Attainment and census.** A containing halfspace can be moved parallel to pass through the mark $(1,0,0,0)$ in the product, with its mass weakly decreasing. If its $x$ coefficient is nonzero, symmetry in $x$ and positive scaling give the margin $x+a(p-1)+bq+v\cdot w\ge0$. Fubini expresses its mass as $\int_L F(a,b,v\cdot w)\,dw$. Symmetry of $L$ and the paired bound give at least $24|L|$. In dimension one set $c=0$, so the paired bound gives $F(a,b,0)\ge24$. In either case, if the $x$ coefficient is zero, add a nonzero $\varepsilon x$ and let $\varepsilon\to0$. The pointwise limit superior of the indicators is bounded by the indicator of the original closed cap, including on its boundary. Reverse Fatou for the finite measure gives the same lower bound. The caps $H_\pm$ attain the upper bound at the mark. Reflection in $p$ gives the other outer mark. Every halfspace containing the midpoint contains at least one endpoint, proving the middle mark is also globally maximizing.

In dimension one, the bottom and top rows have strict upper bounds $15$ and $33/5$. At a middle-row point with $x\ne0$, one of $H_\pm$ has strictly positive margin, and moving its threshold to that point removes positive length from its own interval. For a middle-row point $(j,0,0)$ with $j\ge2$, use $x+t(p-j)\ge0$ with $t>0$. Its limiting bottom contribution at $j=2$ is $5\cdot2+1=11$, its middle contribution is $2\cdot16/5+8/5=8$, and its top contribution is zero. These limits are nonincreasing with $j$, so some finite $t$ has mass below $24$. Reflection excludes $j\le-2$. This proves the exact one-dimensional census.

**Oriented data.** Each $H_\pm$ properly cuts the nine middle and three top fibers. In all fifteen bottom fibers it has one empty-side supporting point of $\mathcal H^0$ measure one. The affine functional $h=(p+1)/2$ equals $0,1$ at the respective outer marks, and the exterior weight summed over the bottom row is $\sum_{p=-7}^7\operatorname{dist}((p+1)/2,[0,1])=\sum_{p=2}^7(p-1)=21$. Thus $12\le21$ for each cap. The continuous normals $1,-1$ balance with coefficients $1/2,1/2$, and the base coefficient of each cap vanishes on the endpoint displacement.
statement:
Use integer coordinates $(p,q)$ and let the compact convex body in continuous dimension one be
$$
C=\{(p,q,x):-1\le q\le1,\ |p|\le4-3q,\ |x|\le8/5+3q/5\}.
$$
Its total mixed volume is $72$. Its global maximum raw closed-halfspace depth is $24$, attained exactly at $(-1,0,0),(0,0,0),(1,0,0)$. For every $d\ge2$ and every centrally symmetric convex body $L\subset\mathbb R^{d-1}$ centered at zero, the body $C\times L$ has total mixed volume $72|L|$ and global maximum raw depth $24|L|$. The same three marks with added continuous coordinate zero attain it. Thus the normalized maximum is $1/3$ in all these dimensions and the outer maximizers have the same integer parity.

In dimension one the two actual caps $\{\pm x+q\ge0\}$ minimize at both outer marks and have opposite unit continuous normals. For $h=(p+1)/2$, each has proper section mass $12$, fifteen empty-side supporting points, no full-side supporting sections and exterior empty-side flux $21$ in counting measure.
title: An actual faceted mixed body with a global same-parity depth plateau
